questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following terms:

i) Homeostasis.

ii) Osmoregulation. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Homeostasis.** The **maintenance of a relatively constant internal environment** (the blood and tissue fluid surrounding the cells: temperature, pH, blood glucose, water potential, oxygen and carbon dioxide levels) **within narrow limits**, in spite of changes outside the body or in the activity of the organism. It works by **negative feedback**: receptors detect a change from the set point, a control centre (e.g. the hypothalamus) compares and effectors reverse the change.

**(ii) Osmoregulation.** The **control of the water potential (osmotic pressure) and the salt and water content of the body fluids** so that they remain constant. In mammals it is carried out mainly by the **kidneys**, under the control of **antidiuretic hormone (ADH)** from the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary, which adjusts the volume and concentration of urine.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain the role played by the following hormones in homeostasis:

i) Insulin.

ii) Calcitonin.

iii) Antidiuretic hormone (ADH). *[12 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Insulin** (regulation of blood glucose)

- Insulin is a **polypeptide hormone** made by the **$\beta$ cells of the islets of Langerhans** of the pancreas. It is released when the **blood glucose concentration rises** (e.g. after a meal), detected by the $\beta$ cells themselves.
- It acts on the **liver, muscle and fat cells**: it makes the cell membranes **more permeable to glucose** (more glucose carrier proteins), activates the enzymes that convert **glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis)** in the liver and muscles, stimulates the conversion of glucose to **fat**, and increases the **oxidation (respiration) of glucose** in cells.
- The **blood glucose falls** back to the normal level (about 90 mg per 100 cm$^3$), and insulin secretion falls (**negative feedback**). Its antagonist is **glucagon** (from the $\alpha$ cells), which raises blood glucose when it is too low. A lack of insulin causes **diabetes mellitus**.

**(ii) Calcitonin** (regulation of blood calcium)

- Calcitonin is made by the **parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid gland** and is released when the **blood calcium (Ca$^{2+}$) concentration is too high**.
- It **lowers the blood calcium level** by **inhibiting the osteoclasts** (reducing the breakdown of bone and release of calcium), by **stimulating the osteoblasts and the deposition of calcium in the bones**, and by **reducing the reabsorption of calcium in the kidney tubules** (more is excreted in the urine) and its absorption in the gut.
- When the level is back to normal, calcitonin secretion falls (negative feedback). Its antagonist is **parathormone**, which raises calcium when it is too low.

**(iii) Antidiuretic hormone, ADH** (regulation of water potential)

- ADH is made by **neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus** and **released from the posterior lobe of the pituitary gland**. It is released when the **osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a low water potential of the blood** (dehydration, much sweating, salty food).
- It acts on the **cells of the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct of the nephron**: it makes their walls **more permeable to water** (more aquaporins inserted). **More water is reabsorbed by osmosis** into the surrounding tissue (the medulla has a low water potential) and the blood, so the kidney produces a **small volume of concentrated urine**, and the water potential of the blood rises towards the normal value.
- If the blood water potential is **high** (much water drunk), less ADH is released, the walls stay impermeable, and a **large volume of dilute urine** is produced. This is **negative feedback**.

questions.enonce_markdown: Why do mammals produce large quantities of urine during fright? *[4 marks]* *(4, 12, 4 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
During fright the body prepares for "fight or flight" and the following happens.

1. The **sympathetic nervous system** and the **adrenal medulla** release **adrenaline (and noradrenaline)**. These raise the heart rate and the **blood pressure**, and **constrict the arterioles of the skin and gut** while dilating those of muscles.
2. The **higher blood pressure in the glomerulus** increases the **rate of ultrafiltration**, so **more filtrate** is formed in the Bowman's capsules than usual.
3. Fright also **inhibits the hypothalamus and the release of ADH** from the posterior pituitary, so the **distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts become less permeable to water**: **less water is reabsorbed** and a **large volume of dilute urine** is produced.
4. Nervous effects also cause **relaxation of the bladder sphincters**, so that urine is released.

The animal loses water, but it is lighter and ready to escape.
